chapter: Learning from players; Jonah Jones lessons
title: Trummy Young, Roy Eldridge and Jonah's dependency
summary: Referrals from Jonah, Clark Terry and Doc Severinson; Maxwell tells Jonah to stop.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Oh, yeah. I had the same thing out in Honolulu, I went out there to play that Louis Armstrong program and Trummy Young asked, he was admiring my endurance and my upper register and everything. He said, you're in your 60's, you're so strong. And I said, well, I've got a good system and he said, oh, yeah, he'd heard about it from Jonah. I guess everybody's heard from Jonah.
Jonah's the type, he appreciates it.
Well, you know, I think I must have one-third of my pupils either from Clark Terry, Jonah Jones or Doc Severinson, because they all recommend me.
That's a good place to come from.

Yeah. Jonah was trying to get Roy to come to me. Roy told me, 'Jonah's been talking about you. What is it?' I said, well, it's a thing I do on the mouthpiece, you know. And right away he said, well, you know, I always practiced on the mouthpiece. And he's got this little mouthpiece that's hollowed out that he does, but it's not the same thing. I have a definite approach, you know, where you have to learn a new embuchure.
And Jonah keeps wanting to come back, you know, he said,

I want to get a sound like you, or something. I said, Jonah, it's time for you to stop. He said, why? I said, why do you want to sound like me. Jonah Jones, you've got a beautiful sound, if you're starting to fool around with your sound, you're through. I don't want any part of that. And I told his manager, it's not good for him to be dependent on me like this, he doesn't need me. I don't know how to explain it, I mean, I don't know what the right way to say it is, but he could screw himself up if he gets some kind of dependency on me. Every-time something goes wrong he thinks I've got to help him, because he's a good trumpet player and he always was, and he's on his own and doing fine now. Like he'll have a problem and I'll ask him, well, didn't you ever have a problem before, and he'll say, sure. And I said, well, you've got it again. You don't need me, do what you did before. You're fine now.

Well, he's eternally grateful. I'm sure he is and I'm sure Buck is too. But, Jimmy, as a pro trumpet player coming to you, even after a guy like Jonah, big man like Jonah, and a star like Roy, it's hard for a professional to realize there is someone like you, who has that kind of humility. And would do what you said, let them have their dignity, you'd be able to do this in such a way that it won't be embarrassing to them.
